| `InfiniteScroll` | `bool` | `false` | Parameter |  | Accumulates rows chunk by chunk as the user reaches the bottom, instead of paging. No pager is shown: this is a paging strategy of its own and it replaces PageSize's. It differs from Virtual in what it asks of the source, which is the whole reason both exist. A virtualized provider is asked for an arbitrary window - "rows 4000 to 4050" - and has to report a total, because the scrollbar cannot be sized without one. This one walks sequentially from the first chunk and learns where the end is by getting a short one, so it works against a source that can neither seek nor count: a cursor- or keyset-paginated API, a search endpoint, anything whose COUNT is too expensive to run per keystroke. Where the source can do both, Virtual is the better answer - it gives a real scrollbar and does not grow without bound. The chunk size is PageSize, or 50 when that is 0 (which means "do not page" and is no answer to "how much to fetch"). Loading stops when a chunk comes back shorter than the chunk size, or when the reported total is reached. Combine with Virtual to recycle what has accumulated - otherwise a long enough scroll ends with the whole set in the DOM. |

### `GetExportData(string fileName)`

Builds the export snapshot for the current grid state: the visible data columns in display order and the full filtered/sorted row set (all pages). Each column carries both the raw value (for structured exporters such as JSON) and type/format-aware display text (for CSV, TSV, Markdown and Excel) matching what the grid renders. Pass the result to an IDataGridExporter, or wire it via DataGridExport.Grid.
Returns: `DataGridExportData<TItem>`.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fileName` | `string` | Base file name (without extension) the exporter applies its own extension to. |
